planting.note: Grow a grafted tree in a bright, south-facing window or outdoors in full sun, letting the soil surface dry slightly between waterings to protect the roots.

directions: Meiwa is considered the sweetest kumquat commonly grown, prized because both the thin rind and the gumball-sized golden-orange flesh are pleasant to eat out of hand rather than needing sugar or cooking. Fragrant white flowers open over summer and the grafted tree, which fruits much sooner than a seedling, carries ripening fruit from roughly December into April. It stays naturally compact, making it well suited to container culture on a sunny patio or bright indoor windowsill through winter. Let the surface inch of soil dry before rewatering, and maximize light exposure to encourage heavier bloom and fruit set.

planting.note: Site a grafted tree where it gets 6-8 hours of direct sun daily and let the top 1-2 inches of soil dry between waterings in well-drained mix.

directions: Changshou, also sold as the Fukushu kumquat, bears larger, rounder, pear-shaped fruit than most kumquats, with a sweet-tart balance and thin rind good for fresh eating, marmalade, or garnish. Small white flowers carry a light citrus fragrance and can open in repeated flushes through the growing season, occasionally yielding more than one fruit set per year. Being naturally compact and precocious as a grafted tree, it begins fruiting within a year or two and stays manageable in a container on a bright patio or sunroom. Keep it in strong, direct light and avoid letting the pot sit wet, since kumquats resent waterlogged roots.

common_name: Smith Red Blood Orange (Anthocyanin-Rich Red-Fleshed Orange)

planting.note: Grow this grafted selection in full sun and expose it to a wide day-to-night temperature swing as fruit matures, since that swing is what deepens the red pigment.

directions: Smith Red was selected in Ventura County, California for an intensely red-pigmented rind and deep red, anthocyanin-rich flesh with a sweet flavor and very few seeds. As a grafted tree it bears earlier and more reliably than a seed-grown blood orange, ripening late winter and holding its fruit on the branch into late spring without quickly declining in quality. Color and sweetness both improve when warm days are followed by distinctly cooler nights, so a patio spot with some nighttime temperature drop helps more than a uniformly warm sunroom. Keep it in full sun with regular water during active growth and fruit swell, tapering off once fruit is ripening.

common_name: Edinburgh Begonia (Malaysian Rainforest Fibrous Begonia with Rose-Red Foliage)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in warm, humid partial sun year-round, moving containers outdoors to a shaded summer spot once nights stay above 65F.

directions: Edinburgh is a striking fibrous begonia selection of Begonia brevirimosa from the rainforests of Malaysia, with large upright leaves washed in vivid rose-red tones. It wants steady warmth and high humidity, performing best as an indoor houseplant through the cooler months and as an accent in a shaded patio planter or window box once summer nights stay reliably above 65F. Keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, and avoid letting indoor temperatures drop much below 65F or growth stalls. Bright, filtered light rather than direct sun keeps the rose-red coloring intense without bleaching the leaves.

common_name: Dragon Shield Begonia (Bornean Rainforest Species with Metallic Textured Leaves)

planting.note: Pot up in a humid terrarium or glass case in partial shade, keeping minimum temperatures above 65F.

directions: Begonia dracopelta comes from the wet tropical rainforests of Borneo and carries dramatically textured, dragon-scale-like foliage that gives the species its name. It is a compact terrarium specialist that flourishes under the sustained high humidity of an enclosed case, with light levels doubling as a color dial: brighter conditions speed growth and push the leaves toward vivid green, while dimmer, shadier spots intensify the dark, metallic sheen it is prized for. Keep it consistently humid and warm, never letting the minimum temperature drop below about 65F, and expect only intermittent, inconspicuous bloom. Because of its small stature and love of still, moist air, it suits a closed glass terrarium far better than open-room houseplant conditions.

planting.note: Treat seed with GA-3 before sowing to break dormancy and raise germination rates in this slow-to-start Solanaceae curiosity.

directions: This South American member of the nightshade family is a sprawling, semi-woody evergreen scrambler rather than an upright border plant, so give it room to ramble over rocks or low supports. Its clustered tubular flowers smell unpleasant on purpose, luring flies in as pollinators, and are followed by flattened green berries among oddly wavy-margined leaves. Because fresh seed germinates slowly and erratically, pretreat with gibberellic acid and expect a one-to-two-month wait even under warmth. Once established in well-drained but moisture-retentive soil it is a long-lived, low-maintenance conversation piece for collectors of botanical oddities.

planting.note: Start in trays and grow on in a container the first year where winters drop much below Zone 7, since it is a Mediterranean island endemic.

directions: Found only on the Mediterranean island of Mallorca, this low, spreading nettle relative is grown strictly for its striking foliage rather than for any culinary use. The leaves have deeply cut, toothed margins and are studded with small raised, inflated spots across the surface, giving the whole plant a textured, almost blistered look unlike the familiar stinging nettle. It stays low and clump-forming, suiting a container or rock-garden niche where its unusual leaf texture can be appreciated up close. Give it a sheltered, humus-rich spot since its island origin leaves it less cold-hardy than its mainland relatives.

common_name: Ololiuqui (Christmas Vine, Giant Tropical Morning-Glory Relative)

planting.note: Nick the hard seed coat and keep warm; grow in a large tub or greenhouse outside truly tropical climates since it is frost-tender and eventually massive.

directions: Also sold under the synonym Turbina corymbosa, this is a large woody twining vine from tropical America that, given years to mature, develops a trunk as thick as a human thigh and can scale tall trees or structures. It produces abundant clusters of white, inch-wide, morning-glory-shaped flowers and bears heart-shaped leaves up to four inches long, and it is valued by beekeepers as a strong honey plant. Historically known to Mesoamerican cultures under the name Ololiuqui, it is grown today purely as an ornamental curiosity for the tropical or large greenhouse garden. Nick the seed before sowing and expect a warm, patient germination before this long-lived vine gets going.

common_name: Lapeirousia (Painted Petals, South African Spike-Flower Corm)

planting.note: Grow like gladiolus corms in light, sharply drained soil, lifting or mulching heavily for winter protection where the ground freezes hard.

directions: Now more correctly classified as Freesia laxa, and previously circulated under the synonym Anamotheca laxa, this diminutive South African corm sends up narrow, foot-long leaves and wiry stems topped with one-sided spikes of six to twelve salmon-pink flowers, each marked with a bold red eye. Though from a mild winter-rainfall climate, it is reported to tolerate surprisingly cold conditions with winter protection, and it naturalizes readily in favorable mild climates such as coastal California. Grow it as you would gladiolus, in light, full-sun soil, and consider it equally at home in open ground or forced in pots under glass. Seed germinates readily but can take a month or more to get going.

common_name: Penn Inn Pippin Apple (Devon Roundabout Seedling)

planting.note: Seed needs a cold stratification period before sowing, and because apples do not come true from seed, expect variable results and several years to first fruit.

directions: This late-season apple was discovered growing wild as a seedling on a roundabout near Newton Abbot, Devon, and produces generous crops of red-blushed golden fruit with soft, sweet flesh. The fruit keeps well into winter when stored properly. Plant in full sun with free-draining soil, and be patient since seed-grown trees take years to establish and bear an unpredictable but often worthwhile harvest. Grafting onto dwarfing rootstock is the usual route for a known, compact tree, but this variety began life as a chance seedling, so growing from seed keeps that spirit alive.

planting.note: Sow indoors in late winter, then train the vigorous canes onto wires or a trellis once plants are established outside.

directions: This blackberry is grown for exceptionally long, fat, juicy fruits on vigorous canes that benefit from being trained in rows along supports. Seedling plants vary somewhat in character, so growing a few and selecting the most productive is worthwhile. It wants full sun and free-draining soil, with fruiting canes typically bearing in their second year. Prune out spent floricanes after harvest to keep the planting productive and manageable.

planting.note: Pre-stratified seed can be sown indoors directly; choose a warm, sheltered site since this South American-bred hybrid fruits late and favors heat.

directions: Bred in Brazil from Comanche and Uruguai parent blackberries, this thorny, upright cane fruit ripens notably late in the season and produces sweet, succulent black berries. It performs best in warm climates with free-draining soil and full sun exposure. Support the upright canes to keep fruiting wood off the ground and ease harvesting. Because it fruits later than most blackberries, it extends the bramble season into early autumn.

planting.note: Grow in gritty, sharply drained soil or a rock garden pocket; this mat-forming plant spreads readily once established.

directions: Originally collected on Chiloé Island off the coast of Chile, this low, evergreen mat-former is grown for its curious plum-sized, spiky brown seed heads that stand up above a carpet of finely divided green-and-silver foliage. It suits rock gardens, gravel paths, and trough plantings where the unusual burrs can be seen up close. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil, since it resents winter waterlogging more than cold. Trim back old foliage in spring to keep the mat looking fresh.
